glossary.definition: A pattern where you search your private documents for relevant facts and paste them into the prompt so the AI reads them instead of guessing from memory.
When an AI does not know the answer but invents a confident, wrong response instead of saying 'I don't know'.
Giving the model explicit text to read and strict instructions to answer only from that text, so it cannot invent facts.

hook.scenario: You ask an internal support bot: 'What is our SLA for enterprise customers?' It confidently answers '99.9%'. The real answer is '99.99%'. Before you read on, predict: did the model lie, or is something else happening?
hook.question: Think about where the model's answer came from — then read on to understand hallucination and how retrieval fixes it.

mental_model.intuition: RAG turns a closed-book exam into an open-book exam. Instead of guessing from memory, the model reads the answer off the page you hand it.
mental_model.description: Standard LLMs answer from weights learned during training. When they do not know the answer, they do not say 'I don't know' — they generate the most likely-sounding next token, which is often wrong. Grounding fixes this: you retrieve the relevant document text and paste it directly into the prompt. The model's job shifts from 'remember the answer' to 'read the answer out of the provided text'.

illustration.alt: An LLM reading relevant pages from an open book to answer, versus a crossed-out closed-book guess.

sections.body: LLMs are excellent at reading, summarizing, and reasoning. They are terrible at storing facts. Their training data has a cutoff date, and they have no knowledge of your private company documents. If you ask a niche or private question, they will confidently hallucinate an answer that sounds right but is wrong.
sections.recap: Models reason well but store facts poorly. Questions about private or recent data produce hallucinations.

sections.body: The fix is to stop relying on the model's memory. Use a search system to find the relevant information, then paste that text directly into the prompt. The model reads the answer instead of guessing. The model's reasoning ability is the same — but now it has the right facts in front of it.
sections.recap: Provide the facts in the prompt so the model reads instead of guessing.

sections.body: This workflow is called Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It has two steps: retrieve the right facts from a database, then generate an answer using only those facts. The pipeline is: User query → Vector search → Retrieve relevant chunks → Inject into prompt → Model reads and replies.
sections.recap: RAG pipeline: Retrieve the facts, Augment the prompt, Generate the answer.

sections.body: The prompt must include strict instructions to anchor the model. You tell it explicitly: 'Answer ONLY using the provided context. If the answer is not in the context, say I don't know.' Without this instruction, the model may combine the retrieved text with hallucinated facts. This explicit instruction is the 'grounding'.
sections.recap: Grounding = context in the prompt + strict instruction to read only from that context.

sections.body: RAG shifts the burden of accuracy from the model to your search system. If the retriever finds the wrong paragraphs, the model gives the wrong answer — or correctly says 'I don't know'. If it finds the right paragraphs, the model almost always succeeds. AI engineers spend most of their time improving retrieval, not the generation step.
sections.recap: The model can only use what the retriever finds. If retrieval fails, the bot fails.

code_snippets.title: Without grounding — hallucination risk
code_snippets.code:
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

# Model guesses from training data — private facts will be hallucinated
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model='gpt-4o',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is the SLA for RetainHQ Enterprise?'}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)  # Likely wrong
code_snippets.explanation: Without context, the model relies on pre-trained weights. For private company data it was never trained on, it will generate a plausible-sounding but incorrect answer.

code_snippets.title: With grounding — model reads the answer instead of guessing
code_snippets.code:
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

# 1. Retrieve the relevant fact (from your vector store, simplified here)
retrieved_docs = 'RetainHQ Enterprise accounts guarantee a 99.99% uptime SLA.'

# 2. Augment the prompt with the context and strict instructions
grounded_prompt = f'''
Answer the question using ONLY the provided context.
If the context does not contain the answer, say "I don't know."

Context:
{retrieved_docs}

Question: What is the SLA for RetainHQ Enterprise?
'''

# 3. Generate the grounded answer
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model='gpt-4o',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': grounded_prompt}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)  # 99.99%
code_snippets.explanation: The model reads the exact fact from the retrieved context. The strict instruction tells it to refuse if the answer is not present — this prevents the model from falling back to hallucination.

key_points.title: Memory vs reading
key_points.detail: LLMs are bad at storing facts but excellent at reading them. Give them the text to read, not the fact to remember.

key_points.title: The RAG pipeline
key_points.detail: Retrieve the facts → Augment the prompt with those facts → Generate the answer.

key_points.title: Strict instructions are required
key_points.detail: Grounding only works if you tell the model to answer only from the context and refuse if the answer is absent.

key_points.title: Retrieval is the bottleneck
key_points.detail: The model can only use what you retrieve. Improving retrieval improves RAG quality more than upgrading the model.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting the 'I don't know' instruction
common_mistakes.explanation: If you paste context without telling the model to restrict itself, it will blend the retrieved text with its own guesses. Add explicit instruction to refuse if the answer is not in the provided context.

common_mistakes.title: Assuming a better model fixes bad retrieval
common_mistakes.explanation: Switching from a small model to GPT-4o will not fix RAG quality if the retriever is returning wrong documents. Improve retrieval first — the model can only answer what is in the prompt.

recall_questions.q: Explain what Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) does, as if to a classmate.
recall_questions.answer: RAG is a technique that searches your documents for relevant facts and pastes them into the prompt before asking the model to answer. Instead of guessing from memory, the model reads the answer from the retrieved text. This prevents hallucination on private or recent information.

recall_questions.q: What are the three steps of the RAG pipeline?
recall_questions.answer: Retrieve relevant facts from a database. Augment the prompt by adding those facts plus strict instructions. Generate the answer — the model reads from the context, not from memory.

recall_questions.q: Why is it important to include an 'I don't know' instruction in a RAG prompt?
recall_questions.answer: If the retriever finds no relevant context, the model needs permission to refuse. Without this instruction, the model will try to be helpful and generate a hallucinated answer instead of admitting it does not know.

recall_questions.q: Your RAG bot answers wrong for a specific topic. Should you upgrade the model first? Predict what the most likely root cause is.
recall_questions.answer: Probably not. Most RAG failures are retrieval failures — the right documents were not found, so the model had nothing accurate to read. Upgrade the retrieval (better chunking, better embedding model, or reranking) before switching the generation model.

oa_questions.question: A team's RAG chatbot still hallucinates on questions about features that do not exist. How would you debug and fix this?
oa_questions.answer: The model is falling back to its internal knowledge when the retriever returns nothing. Two fixes: first, add explicit grounding instructions ('Answer ONLY from the provided context, otherwise say I don't know'). Second, add a minimum similarity threshold so that a low-quality retrieval returns zero chunks — which forces the model into its 'I don't know' fallback state.
oa_questions.approach: Identify the model falling back to internal knowledge as the root cause. The two fixes are grounding instructions and a similarity threshold to trigger the refusal path explicitly.

oa_questions.question: You have a large corpus of private documents and want to build a Q&A bot. Should you fine-tune the model on the documents or use RAG?
oa_questions.answer: Use RAG. Fine-tuning is for teaching a model a new style, format, or reasoning pattern — it is poor at memorizing new facts and still hallucinates them confidently. RAG is cheaper, lets you update or delete documents without retraining, provides citations, and prevents hallucination through grounding.
oa_questions.approach: Contrast fact retrieval (RAG) vs behavior modification (fine-tuning). Fine-tuning does not reliably store new facts. RAG is the correct tool for document Q&A.
